stories.title: Goldman Sachs Affiliate Sells 303K-SF Phoenix Retail Center
stories.excerpt: Goldman Sachs Asset Management has offloaded Grand Canyon Crossing, a 303,000 square foot Phoenix shopping center. Cohen & Steers Income Opportunities REIT Inc, along with the Sterling Organization, was the buyer. Commercial Search reports that the project was completed in 2005. The center is 99 percent occupied and anchored by a 207,000-square-foot Walmart Supercenter. Grand Canyon Crossing’s tenants also include Harbor Freight, Starbucks, Wendy’s, Jamba Juice and Sonic. Grand Canyon Crossing is situated on 33 acres at Bethany Home Road and 35th Avenue. Grand Canyon University is about 1.5 miles away. The Sterling Organization says it is a vertically integrated private equity real estate firm whose national platform is focused on investing in retail and distribution real estate assets across the risk spectrum in major markets within the United States. The post Goldman Sachs Affiliate Sells 303K-SF Phoenix Retail Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Goldman Sachs sells 303K-SF Phoenix retail center (Grand Canyon Crossing) 99% occupied.
Cohen & Steers Income Opportunities REIT and Sterling Organization acquire asset completed 2005.
Property anchored by 207K-SF Walmart; 1.5 miles from Grand Canyon University.
stories.summary: Goldman Sachs Asset Management divested Grand Canyon Crossing, a 303,000-square-foot Phoenix retail center completed in 2005, to Cohen & Steers Income Opportunities REIT and Sterling Organization. The 33-acre property is 99% leased and anchored by a 207,000-square-foot Walmart Supercenter, with additional tenants including Harbor Freight, Starbucks, and quick-service restaurants. The asset sits near Grand Canyon University on Bethany Home Road and 35th Avenue.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Retail asset sale does not signal demand or supply shifts affecting apartment markets. However, persistent institutional appetite for stabilized, high-occupancy retail (especially Walmart-anchored centers) reflects continued consumer spending confidence in Phoenix, which supports underlying household formation and rental demand in the metro.

stories.title: Twin Cities Accounting Firm Consolidates Offices Into 43K-SF Space
stories.excerpt: Carlson Partners announced that its advisors, Tim Olsen, SIOR, partner, and Sami Cowger, SIOR, executive director, represented Boyum Barenscheer, a Twin Cities accounting and advisory firm, in consolidating its two Minnesota offices into a new headquarters at Midway Innovation Center II, 2344 Energy Park Drive in St. Paul.Boyum Barenscheer previously operated from an office at 3050 Metro Drive in Bloomington and a second office at 1210 W. County Road E in Arden Hills. The new headquarters spans 43,346 square feet, an increase of more than 6,000 square feet over the firm’s combined previous footprint and gives Boyum Barenscheer a central location to bring its Bloomington and Arden Hills offices together under one roof. The firm will occupy two of the building’s three floors.The landlord, CSM, was represented by Transwestern‘s Eric Rapp, SIOR, and JLL’s Eric Batiza, SIOR. Carlson Partners represented Boyum Barenscheer throughout the entire real estate process, from site selection through lease negotiations and continues to advise the firm through design, buildout and move-in. The post Twin Cities Accounting Firm Consolidates Offices Into 43K-SF Space appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Twin Cities accounting firm Boyum Barenscheer consolidates two offices into 43K-SF HQ.
Firm moves from Bloomington and Arden Hills to Midway Innovation Center II, St. Paul.
New space is 6K-SF larger than combined prior footprint; represents office flight to mixed-use.
stories.summary: Boyum Barenscheer, a Twin Cities accounting and advisory firm, consolidated its two Minnesota offices (previously in Bloomington and Arden Hills) into a new 43,346-square-foot headquarters at Midway Innovation Center II in St. Paul. The consolidation adds approximately 6,000 square feet to the firm's combined prior office footprint. Carlson Partners' advisors Tim Olsen and Sami Cowger represented the firm in the transaction.
stories.impact: Flight of professional services tenants from suburban office parks (Bloomington, Arden Hills) to mixed-use innovation centers signals ongoing flight-to-quality in Twin Cities office market, reducing traditional suburban office demand. This trend typically correlates with young professional talent preference for walkable, mixed-use locations with residential proximity—subtle signal to develop or acquire multifamily near urban innovation districts (St. Paul's Midway) rather than suburban office parks.

stories.title: Samsung Commits $1B to Helix’s Digital Infrastructure Strategy
stories.excerpt: Helix Digital Infrastructure and KKR announced that Samsung has committed $1 billion to Helix, an AI infrastructure company formed by KKR this past June to help meet the growing infrastructure needs of hyperscalers, through its long-duration capital fund. Samsung’s investment builds on the more than $10 billion of capital committed to the Helix strategy at its launch by founding investors including KKR, the Kuwait Investment Authority, NVIDIA and Vistra. The new commitment will provide additional long-duration capital to support Helix’s strategy of investing in and delivering the data centers, power, connectivity and related infrastructure that are required to support growing AI demand. “Samsung’s commitment is a strong vote of confidence in Helix’s strategy and further deepens the long-term capital base we’ve built to meet the scale of AI infrastructure demand,” said Adam Selipsky, CEO and co-founder, Helix. “As one of the world’s leading technology companies, Samsung brings unique capabilities that we expect will benefit Helix and its customers, and we look forward to working together to accelerate the deployment of next-generation digital infrastructure for hyperscalers around the world.” The post Samsung Commits $1B to Helix’s Digital Infrastructure Strategy appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Samsung commits $1B to Helix Digital Infrastructure (KKR-founded AI infrastructure platform).
Total Helix capital raised now exceeds $11B; backing data center and power buildout.
Capital supports hyperscaler AI demand; nationwide implications for data center siting and power.
stories.summary: Samsung announced a $1 billion commitment to Helix Digital Infrastructure, an AI infrastructure company formed by KKR in June 2024. Helix, which has now raised more than $11 billion from KKR, Kuwait Investment Authority, NVIDIA, Vistra, and now Samsung, will deploy capital to build data centers, power infrastructure, and connectivity required by hyperscalers. The long-duration capital structure positions Helix to accelerate deployment of next-generation digital infrastructure.
stories.impact: Massive influx of capital into AI data center buildout will intensify demand for power, land, and logistics infrastructure in select metros (Texas, Virginia, Arizona, California). This indirectly signals sustained tech employment and population inflows to data center hubs; multifamily developers should acquire land or pipeline projects in secondary markets with favorable power costs and logistics access (e.g., North Texas, Central Valley CA, Arizona) ahead of data center hyperscaler relocations and their talent followings.

stories.title: Burlington Stores Inks 32K SF at Brooklyn Navy Yard’s Admirals Row Campus
stories.excerpt: Burlington Stores is coming to the Brooklyn Navy Yard. The retailer formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory signed a 31,717-square-foot retail lease at 25 Navy Street, according to city records filed Tuesday evening. The vacant two-story development between Sands Street and Flushing Avenue borders the Wegmans-anchored shopping center at Admiral’s Row, an 8-acre mixed-use campus developed by Doug Steiner’s development arm, Steiner NYC. Burlington’s Navy Street lease spans an 11,385-square-foot portion of ground-floor space and the entire 20,332-square-foot second floor. Its upcoming occupancy at the under-construction building leaves 7,000 square feet still available, according to marketing materials. Steiner said in a statement to Commercial Observer that Steiner NYC is “thrilled to welcome Burlington.” “They’re a fantastic off-price retailer,” Steiner said. “Opening is planned for fall 2027.” Ripco Real Estate’s Jason Pennington and Ben Weiner represented Steiner in the deal, which carries a 10-year term with options to renew. Cliff Simon of CNS Real Estate negotiated on behalf of Burlington. Asking rent was not disclosed, but asking rents along nearby shopping corridors in Downtown Brooklyn averaged $190 per square foot in the first half of 2025, according to the most recent Brooklyn retail data available from the Real Estate Board of New York. Burlington has had a busy 18 months. The company took over 45 leases from bankrupt fabric retailer Joann in May 2025, including at 535 Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. It leased another 43,000-square-foot space at the planned 72-22 Broadway development in Jackson Heights, Queens, in October 2025, and recently opened its doors at 54-23 Myrtle Avenue, part of an embattled mixed-use tower development in Queens’ Ridgewood neighborhood. bullets: Burlington Stores leases 31.7K-SF at Brooklyn Navy Yard's Admirals Row mixed-use campus.
Occupancy spans ground and second floor; opening planned fall 2027; 7K-SF remains unlet.
Doug Steiner's Steiner NYC developed 8-acre campus anchored by Wegmans; borders Navy Yard.
stories.summary: Burlington Stores signed a 31,717-square-foot retail lease at 25 Navy Street, part of the Admirals Row mixed-use campus at Brooklyn Navy Yard developed by Steiner NYC. The lease covers 11,385 square feet of ground-floor space and the entire 20,332-square-foot second floor on a 10-year term with options. Steiner NYC expects the off-price retailer to open fall 2027; 7,000 square feet of the building remains available for lease.
stories.impact: Brooklyn Navy Yard mixed-use development signals sustained retail and ground-floor activation in NYC waterfront submarkets; successful Wegmans + Burton leasing validates neighborhood density and foot traffic. For multifamily, this confirms strong demand fundamentals for residential in nearby Navy Yard/DUMBO submarkets and justifies premium pricing for ground-floor retail-lined residential buildings; monitor adjacent land parcels for residential development opportunities within the 8-acre campus or surrounding area.

stories.title: Quantum Real Estate Advisors Brokers Sale of New Construction Strip Center in Huntley
stories.excerpt: Quantum Real Estate Advisors, Inc. has brokered the sale of a roughly 6,375-square-foot new construction strip center for $2.8 million. The property is located at 12860 IL-47 in Huntley, Illinois, and consists of three suites, with a diverse tenant lineup featuring local and national tenants, including Jimmy John’s and JC Licht. The purchaser is an investor based in the Midwest. The seller, Core Acquisitions, is a Chicago-based developer and shopping center owner. Chad Firsel, President, and Brett Berlin, Senior Vice President, represented the seller in the transaction.“Quality strip center product continues to see strong demand from buyers,” said Berlin. “The buyer was drawn to the asset because of the growth in the Huntley market, driven by new homes and retail development, as well as the opportunity to acquire a new construction asset at an attractive basis.” Quantum Real Estate Advisors is a commercial real estate brokerage specializing in investment sales and full-service leasing. The post Quantum Real Estate Advisors Brokers Sale of New Construction Strip Center in Huntley appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: New construction strip center in Huntley, Illinois sells for $2.8M (6,375 SF).
Tenants include Jimmy John's and JC Licht; Midwest investor acquires from Core Acquisitions.
Core Acquisitions (Chicago developer) offloads property amid strong buyer demand for quality strip.
stories.summary: Quantum Real Estate Advisors brokered the sale of a 6,375-square-foot new construction strip center at 12860 IL-47 in Huntley, Illinois for $2.8 million. The property features three suites leased to a diverse mix of local and national tenants including Jimmy John's and JC Licht. A Midwest-based investor purchased the asset from Chicago-based developer Core Acquisitions; brokers noted strong buyer appetite for quality strip center product.
stories.impact: Low-friction sale of new-construction retail in suburban Chicago ring signals continued investor appetite for stabilized strip centers with national and local tenants in car-dependent suburbs. Does not directly impact multifamily unless it indicates household density/growth in Huntley submarket (northwest Chicago exurb), which would suggest opportunity for multifamily infill near retail anchors. Limited broader signal.

stories.title: Pierce County to Fund Five Affordable Housing Projects Across the Region
stories.excerpt: Pierce County Human Services is investing $11.4 million to fund five affordable housing projects across the region, adding and preserving 220 affordable homes. The new funding pushes the total supported by the Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Act to 1,545 affordable homes built or preserved since the County began collecting the one-tenth of 1% local sales tax in mid 2023. “These new affordable housing units will provide stability for hundreds of people across Pierce County,” Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello said. “The Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Act continues to make a real difference for our most vulnerable residents and working families.” The new projects target a wide range of housing needs in both urban and suburban areas, including new construction and rehabilitation projects. Pierce County is also improving access to housing by approving new cottage housing regulations that create a pathway for smaller, more affordable homes and securing $2.7 million in state funding to cover essential infrastructure. The post Pierce County to Fund Five Affordable Housing Projects Across the Region appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pierce County, Washington invests $11.4M to fund five affordable housing projects.
Initiative adds/preserves 220 affordable units across region; total Maureen Howard Act funding now 1,545 units.
Funding sourced from 0.1% local sales tax; includes new construction, rehab, and cottage housing regulations.
stories.summary: Pierce County Human Services is investing $11.4 million to fund five affordable housing projects that will add and preserve 220 affordable homes across the region. The funding brings the total supported by the Maureen Howard Affordable Housing Act—funded by a 0.1% local sales tax implemented in mid-2023—to 1,545 affordable units. New projects include both new construction and rehabilitation in urban and suburban areas, plus $2.7 million in state funding for infrastructure and new cottage housing regulations.
stories.impact: Aggressive local public funding for affordable housing in Pierce County (Tacoma, Olympia area) reduces development feasibility and returns for market-rate multifamily in the region by increasing supply of deed-restricted competition and tightening the spread between rents and development costs. Developers should monitor if this accelerates zoning/cottage housing approvals that could enable smaller-unit, lower-cost-per-door multifamily development (co-living, micro apartments) or shift focus to higher-barrier markets (Seattle, Bellevue) where public subsidy is less abundant.

stories.title: Ken Griffin Gives $3B to Carnegie Mellon to Launch 35-Acre Miami Campus
stories.excerpt: Billionaire Ken Griffin is making a $3 billion donation to Carnegie Mellon University, including $2 billion to build a major new campus in Miami’s Wynwood neighborhood. It’s the largest single donation to higher education by one person, according to an announcement from Carnegie Mellon. Griffin will also give $1 billion to the university’s Pittsburgh campus, while joining its board of trustees. The Miami campus will span 35 acres and focus on computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and other tech sectors. Carnegie Mellon expects the campus to eventually support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master’s and Ph.D. students, nearly 300 faculty members and more than 600 staff, the announcement said. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with the first students expected in 2028. The university acquired the site from Miami developer Moishe Mana for an undisclosed price, though it has not disclosed who will ultimately hold title to the property. The project represents Carnegie Mellon’s largest expansion beyond its Pittsburgh base. The university currently operates smaller satellite campuses in New York City, Mountain View, Calif., and Qatar. The Miami program will focus on areas including human health, national security, energy and climate resilience, advanced manufacturing and industrial transformation, which will be integrated with AI, computing and machine learning. “The students who graduate and the tech companies that come to Miami to leverage those skills will change the very fabric of Miami for decades, if not centuries, to come,” Griffin said. The campus also deepens Griffin’s investment in Wynwood. He previously partnered with Goldman Properties to acquire a nearby office tower from Sterling Bay for $180 million. That building houses MIAX Sapphire’s 38,400-square-foot options trading floor, along with PwC, Gensler and Sony Music. Griffin has now donated $2.4 billion in South Florida and more than $5.7 billion overall, according to the announcemen
bullets: Ken Griffin donates $3B to Carnegie Mellon: $2B for Miami Wynwood campus, $1B for Pittsburgh.
Miami campus (35 acres) to support 3,500+ students, 300 faculty, 600+ staff by 2028.
Focus on CS, AI, robotics; construction begins 2026; site acquired from Moishe Mana.
stories.summary: Billionaire Ken Griffin donated $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University—the largest single donation to higher education. Of this, $2 billion will fund a new 35-acre campus in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood focused on computer science, artificial intelligence, and robotics. Carnegie Mellon acquired the site from Miami developer Moishe Mana and expects to enroll 3,500+ students, 300 faculty, and 600+ staff, with construction beginning in 2026 and first students arriving in 2028. The university also received $1 billion for its Pittsburgh campus.
stories.impact: Transformational demand signal for Miami multifamily. A 3,500-person influx of university students, faculty, and staff into Wynwood by 2028 will drive sustained renter demand for both on-campus and nearby off-campus housing. Tech-focused graduate and PhD programs attract higher-earning tenants and faculty. Developers should acquire or option land within 0.5–1.5 miles of the 35-acre campus (Wynwood, adjacent neighborhoods) for student and early-career housing; expect rents to rise as supply lags inflow. Secondary effect: prestige tech research institution will attract corporate R&D and startup talent to Miami, expanding broader metro job base and household formation beyond campus.

stories.title: New York-Area Home Sales Dip Slightly Year-Over-Year as Overall Inventory Shrinks
stories.excerpt: Home sales in the New York metropolitan area — defined by the U.S. Census Bureau as 23 counties across New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania — are holding up better than the rest of the country, according to the latest research from Homes.com. Sales in the area slipped just 2.8 percent in August when compared to the same month last year. Nationally, home sales dropped 4.3 percent year-over-year in August. The New York area’s housing market ranks sixth out of the top 40 national markets for its annual sales activity change, according to the Homes.com research. Sellers in the New York metro continue to list homes, with new listings rising 10.3 percent year-over-year to 5,694. However, overall inventory in the area dropped 3.1 percent, which is well behind the national benchmark gain of 5.4 percent. The New York metro area’s inventory of homes for sale — 22,336 — also remains 30.7 percent below pre-pandemic levels. “A wave of fresh listings couldn’t stop inventory from shrinking,” Victor Rodriguez, senior director of market analytics at Homes.com, wrote in the report. “Price growth cooled from a year ago, but competition for homes stayed strong.” Home prices are also on the rise, but they aren’t increasing at alarming speeds, according to the research. The median home sales price in the counties encompassing the New York metro area rose 3.3 percent over the past year to $785,000 in August, which exceeded the national benchmark increase of 2.1 percent. Mortgage prices will be the wild card as the year winds down. “The average weekly mortgage rate jumped to 6.95 percent in September, the highest it’s been since January 2025,” Rodriguez wrote. “Some buyers may feel the squeeze of higher borrowing costs in the months to come.” Amanda Schiavo can be reached at aschiavo@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: NY metro area home sales declined 2.8% YoY in August; nationally dropped 4.3%.
NY area ranks 6th nationally for sales activity; overall inventory down 3.1% despite new listings up 10.3%.
NY area inventory 30.7% below pre-pandemic levels; prices cooled but competition remains strong.
stories.summary: New York metropolitan area home sales declined 2.8% year-over-year in August, outperforming the national decline of 4.3%. New listings rose 10.3% year-over-year, but overall inventory fell 3.1%, lagging the national inventory gain of 5.4%. The NY area ranks sixth nationally in annual sales activity change, with inventory at 22,336 homes—30.7% below pre-pandemic levels. Price growth cooled from a year ago, but competition for homes remained strong.
stories.impact: Persistent inventory shortage in NY metro (30.7% below pre-pandemic) signals structurally constrained for-sale housing supply, which sustains rental demand and supports multifamily rent growth and absorption. While home sales are cooling slightly, the inability of sellers to list inventory suggests sticky owner occupancy (low rates locked in, reluctance to sell) and continued renter pool. For-sale weakness does not translate to apartment weakness in supply-constrained NYC metro. Developers should maintain confidence in multifamily fundamentals and focus underwriting on rental-rate stability rather than competing with slower home sales.

stories.title: Citizens Bank Leads $78M Financing on Philly-Area Affordable Housing Rehab
stories.excerpt: Development firm People Restoring Communities (PRC) has sealed $77.61 million in construction financing for the rehabilitation of an affordable housing community in southern New Jersey, Commercial Observer has learned. Citizens Bank provided a $35.85 million construction loan for PRC’s 150-unit Paulsboro Gardens Apartments property in Paulsboro, N.J., just south of Philadelphia to facilitate renovations of the 1968-built complex. The capital stack also features a $23.73 million Freddie Mac-backed tax-exempt loan originated by BWE and $18.03 million in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity syndicated by Enterprise Community Partners. White Plains, N.Y.-based PRC acquired Paulsboro Gardens in July 2025 and received a $20.65 million acquisition loan from X-Caliber, as CO first reported at the time. It marked PRC’s first deal outside of New York state. “When we acquired Paulsboro Gardens last year, we saw an opportunity to create a stronger, more welcoming place for the people who call this community home,” Matthew Linde, principal and CEO of PRC, said in a statement. “The investment reflects our commitment to thoughtful, resident-focused revitalization.” Located at 1A Baird Avenue 14 miles southwest of Downtown Philadelphia, the property consists of 21 low-rise residential buildings with one- and two-bedroom units that will undergo interior improvements as part of the rehabilitation project slated for completion in late 2027. PRC is also planning accessibility upgrades to make the complex more handicapped-accessible along with upgrading the property’s sewer and water infrastructure. Ilya Weinstein, senior vice president at BWE, said in a statement that the financing “allows PRC to move into the next phase of the project.” Citizens Bank and Enterprise Community Partners did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Citizens Bank leads $77.6M construction financing for 150-unit affordable housing rehab in Paulsboro, NJ.
Capital stack: $35.85M Citizens construction loan, $23.73M Freddie Mac tax-exempt, $18.03M LIHTC equity.
PRC acquired property in July 2025; rehab of 1968-built complex; first deal outside NY for developer.
stories.summary: People Restoring Communities (PRC) secured $77.61 million in construction financing for the rehabilitation of Paulsboro Gardens Apartments, a 150-unit property in Paulsboro, New Jersey, just south of Philadelphia. Citizens Bank provided a $35.85 million construction loan, complemented by a $23.73 million Freddie Mac-backed tax-exempt loan and $18.03 million in Low-Income Housing Tax Credit equity from Enterprise Community Partners. PRC acquired the 1968-built property in July 2025 and marked its first deal outside New York state.
stories.impact: Affordable housing re-lending activity in South Jersey (Philadelphia exurb) reflects strong LIHTC equity appetite and Freddie Mac appetite for tax-exempt multifamily debt; signals lender confidence in stabilized rehab economics. For market-rate developers, this indicates solid financing availability for value-add multifamily near Philadelphia. Also signals PRC's geographic expansion strategy into Philadelphia region—watch for competitive affordable development that may pressure market-rate rents if projects are in overlapping submarkets. Monitor for more institutional affordable developer moves into PA/NJ as NYC market matures.

stories.title: In Multifamily, AI Is What You Make It: Forum
stories.excerpt: The age of artificial intelligence has real estate leaders rethinking how they address both the problems of the businesses they run and the clients they serve. The multifamily sector particularly has embraced AI, resulting in questions about how owners in this field use it to scale, consolidate technology stacks, and preserve the human-centered business experience. On Tuesday, Commercial Observer’s executive editor, Cathy Cunningham, hosted a virtual conference — AI & Innovation Forum: Reimagining Multifamily Through AI, Experience & Data — in which experts across multifamily real estate discussed their firms’ approaches to AI utilization and optimization. The forum was broken into three sessions focused on how AI can be used to drive business efficiency and better serve residents. The first panel was moderated by Annie Laurie McCulloh, executive director of leasing and loyalty at Bilt, a rewards platform for renters and homeowners. McCulloh led a discussion between OJ Loor, vice president of systems and integrations at the Bainbridge Companies; Andrew Min, senior vice president of digital and strategic initiatives at RXR; and Don Oldham, vice president of information technology at developer Thompson Thrift. Commercial Observer’s virtual AI Forum. Clockwise from top left: Annie Laurie McCulloh, Andrew Min, Donald Oldham and OJ Loor. bullets: Commercial Observer hosts AI & Innovation Forum focused on multifamily AI adoption and optimization.
Panel discussion covers business efficiency, resident experience, technology stack consolidation.
Multifamily sector leading real estate in AI deployment; focus on scaling and human-centered service.
stories.summary: Commercial Observer hosted a virtual AI & Innovation Forum on multifamily's adoption of artificial intelligence. Panelists from across the sector discussed how owners use AI to drive business efficiency, consolidate technology stacks, and preserve human-centered resident experience. The conference featured three sessions moderated by industry leaders including Annie Laurie McCulloh (Bilt) and included discussion of leasing, operations, and data optimization.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on physical development or market fundamentals. This is industry thought leadership / best-practices discussion. However, the finding that multifamily is leading real estate in AI adoption may indicate competitive pressure on operators to adopt resident-facing and back-office tech; developers should factor 'tech-ready' infrastructure (broadband, smart-home wiring, data platforms) into new product design and operational projections, as tenant expectations for AI-driven leasing, service, and community management are rising. May also signal that operators are optimizing labor productivity via AI, which could support margin resilience in softening rent environments.
